tldr: ToolGen integrates tool retrieval and execution directly into an LLM's generative process by representing each tool as a unique virtual token, eliminating the need for separate retrieval mechanisms.
contributions: A novel framework, ToolGen, that integrates tool retrieval and execution into the LLM's generative process using virtual tokens.
A three-stage training process (tool memorization, retrieval training, and end-to-end agent-tuning) enabling efficient and scalable tool retrieval and API calling.

Experimental validation on 47,000 tools demonstrating comparable performance to current best retrieval methods with significantly less cost and higher efficiency, surpassing traditional tool learning paradigms.
methods: ToolGen maps each tool to a unique virtual token via atomic indexing, expanding the LLM vocabulary by 46,985 tokens. It undergoes three training stages: (1) tool memorization, where the LLM learns to predict tool tokens from tool descriptions; (2) retrieval training, where the model learns to generate relevant tool tokens from user queries; and (3) end-to-end agent-tuning, fine-tuned on task completion trajectories. Constrained beam search restricts output tokens to the predefined tool token set during inference. Experiments used Llama-3-8B as the foundation model, trained with 8 epochs for memorization and 1 epoch for retrieval on 4x A100 GPUs, evaluated on the ToolBench dataset of 47,000 APIs.
results: On the ToolBench dataset with 47,000 tools, ToolGen achieved strong retrieval performance across both In-Domain and Multi-Domain settings. In In-Domain retrieval, ToolGen achieved NDCG@5 scores of 92.67 (domain I1), 91.13 (domain I2), and 90.16 (domain I3), outperforming ToolRetriever (84.39, 70.35, 64.70) and matching or exceeding IterFeedback. In Multi-Domain retrieval, ToolGen achieved NDCG@5 scores of 91.54, 88.84, and 84.79 across domains, substantially outperforming ToolRetriever (74.99, 63.61, 42.92). Atomic indexing was shown to be more efficient and hallucination-resistant than numeric, hierarchical, or semantic indexing alternatives.
limitations: Expanding the vocabulary by ~47,000 tokens increases model size and introduces computational overhead. The constrained beam search, while reducing hallucination, imposes generation constraints. Performance drops in Multi-Domain settings compared to In-Domain, reflecting increased task complexity. The tool memorization and retrieval stages still rely on supervision from existing datasets. Unsupervised baselines (BM25, EmbSim, Re-Invoke) significantly underperform trained methods, indicating dependence on training data.
